method: free-flying wild bats recorded with a microphone array (successive call directions compared); single-microphone recordings in open space gave call amplitude differences between successive calls (mean 8.1 +/- 5.3 dB, up to 24 dB)
conditions: wild common pipistrelles in search flight at edge sites (forest road, farm, garden) in central France and in open space near Tubingen, Germany; number of bats not stated (abstract reports 33 flight sequences, Methods 32; calls analysed given as 725 in one place and 402 in another); sex not reported; the authors note that scanning angles in the abstract were often larger than the maximum angle measurable by the array, so 42 degrees is a floor set by the array, not the animals' maximum; sequences with irregular or no scanning movement were also recorded; successive calls pointing the same way score 0 degrees; pseudoreplication across individuals cannot be completely excluded (authors); this is emission behaviour of the call beam, not a hearing or detection threshold

conditions: captive greater horseshoe bats, printed as Rhinolophus ferrumequinum tragatus, 8 bats analysed (6 males, 2 females) from a colony of 29 housed in a bat facility (colony originated in northern China); all bats combined: mean variation of RF peak frequency over the whole observation period 693.8 +/- 352.98 Hz (n = 1754 calls) against 245.0 +/- 78.19 Hz for SCF (n = 4275), about 35% of the RF variation (+/- most likely SD, not defined in the text); the study did not play back or mask sound, so feedback control is inferred from natural day-to-day variation, not tested; the authors note an observation period of under a week for some analyses is short; RF call peak frequencies before an SCF sequence did not differ significantly, and call durations always differed significantly between days for both call types
